input: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures, and the results that were obtained are summarised as follows. At 300 K, the measured value of $k$ was 0.043 s⁻¹. At 340 K, the value of $k$ was 0.603 s⁻¹, although it should be noted that this second value was not measured directly but was instead computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 56 kJ mol⁻¹, and it is therefore a derived value rather than a direct experimental observation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ across the replicate measurements was found to be 4%, which gives some indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. The measurements at the lower temperature were perfectly satisfactory in this respect, and the derived value at 340 K is quoted alongside them so that the temperature dependence of the reaction can be appreciated over the range which the experiments were able to cover, it being understood that the figure is a calculated rather than an observed one and that it consequently stands or falls with the activation energy on which the calculation was based. Considerable care was taken with the sampling procedure, since any loss of solvent or any delay in dealing with the sample would have distorted the concentrations on which the rate constants are based. It is also worth mentioning that no rate constant is reported for temperatures above 340 K, because at higher temperatures the solvent unfortunately evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to obtain reliable samples under those conditions.
target: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.043 s⁻¹. At 340 K, $k$ = 0.603 s⁻¹, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 56 kJ mol⁻¹ and stated as a derived value, not a measurement. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. The increase between the two temperatures is large, and it is the activation energy that sets it: the derived value at the higher temperature carries the activation energy as an input, so the pair of values is a measurement at the lower temperature extended by the Arrhenius relation, not two independent measurements of the temperature dependence. The replicate spread bounds the measured value only; the derived value inherits that spread and adds whatever error the activation energy itself carries. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K: the absence is a limit of the sampling method at high temperature, not a measurement of the rate there. Sampling is the step the measurement stands on: a sample delayed or partly evaporated returns a concentration the reaction never had, and the rate constant calculated from it inherits the error. The triplicate design is what makes the spread a property of the measurement rather than a guess. The temperature dependence of the reaction is therefore established at the measured point and extended, on the stated basis, to the top of the reported range. The pair of values, one measured and one derived, is the complete record: within the reported range the temperature dependence is quantified, and outside it the reaction may be faster or slower than any extension of the relation would suggest, because the relation has not been tested there. That limit is part of the result and travels with the numbers wherever they are used.
